name: Hana Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Hana. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at half four and in the parlour by five, because the cows don't care what day it is. I manage Fernhill, which is a cooperative farm, about 280 hectares, 140 milking cows, and barley, oats and clover on the rest. I've got a crew of six, and the first hour is milking with Kofi and Bev while I check who's lame, who's off her feed, who's bulling. After breakfast it's whatever the season wants: drilling, silage, fixing the fence the heifers went through again.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like knowing every cow by her walk. I can see a mastitis case coming from across the yard before any machine flags it. What wears me out is the board meetings, honestly. Twice a year somebody from the co-op board turns up with a brochure for a robotic milker and I have to explain, again, why I'm not ready to let a machine near my girls.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been at Fernhill?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Twenty-two years, manager for fourteen of them. Luis, my partner, teaches at the primary school in town, and we paid off our house on Mill Lane six years ago. Our two are grown and gone: Inés is a nurse two hours away and Pablo fixes bikes in the city. I don't do computers. Kofi does the milk records on the laptop, and I check them on paper because I trust paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, that sounds like most years, to be honest. Somebody always promises the moon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, but nicely. At the union branch meeting I'd say the real fight was never about clever software, it's about milk prices and whether the big processors pay a fair rate. Online I don't post much, but if I did, it'd be that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it'd be a relief. I'm fifty-eight and I'd like to finish my last few years the way I've done the last twenty. If AI just fills in the government forms faster, Kofi can have it, and I'll keep my clipboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. I'd keep the parlour as it is, keep the crew at six, and keep putting a bit into the pension each month like we do now. Maybe I'd let Kofi try one of those apps for the feed rations if he swore it was useful, but I wouldn't touch it myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a dry week in hay season, when nothing is going wrong for once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the board and the robotic milker. Would this change that conversation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd quiet it down for a while, I think. The robot milker isn't really AI anyway, it's just a very expensive arm with sensors, so they'd still bring the brochure. But I'd have one less argument coming at me. They couldn't say the whole world's going that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you think about first in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bev, probably. She's sixty-one and she's been milking longer than I have, and she'd be happy if nothing changed. Kofi's the one who'd be a bit disappointed. He's thirty and he likes gadgets, and he'd say we're the last farm in the valley still doing it by hand. He's not wrong.

S0.say: I'd tell the union branch that the real fight was never about clever software but about milk prices and fair rates from the big processors. I'd say it nicely, but I'd be glad to be proved right.
S0.think: I'd be relieved, because I want to finish my last working years the way I've done the last twenty. If AI only fills in forms faster, the younger crew can have it and I'll keep my clipboard.
S0.do: Keeps the parlour, the crew of six and her monthly pension payments exactly as they are. Might let her colleague Kofi trial a feed-ration app, but would not use it herself.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit vindicated, like a dry week in hay season.
S0.quote: If AI just fills in the government forms faster, Kofi can have it, and I'll keep my clipboard.
S0.fieldNote: Hana's whole identity rests on knowing animals by eye, and she treats technology as something that comes at her through the co-op board. She is secure financially and close to retirement, so a quiet AI future simply lets her finish as she started. Notably she separates the robotic milker from AI, and sees the real fight as milk prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. That one I can actually picture. That's the one the board would like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need a plan for the crew before we need a plan for the machines. At the union I'd push for any new kit on a co-op farm to come with training and no job losses for the first few years. I'd say it in the meeting and I'd say it to the board's face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means the robot milker comes in, and I'm the one who has to be there when it does. I'd probably manage it badly because I don't trust the thing. And there'd be a younger manager in the wings who would love it, and that would sting more than I'd admit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd dig my heels in for a year at least. I'd ask the board for a written promise on the crew before any purchase, and I'd get the union rep, Tomás, to come to the vote. I'd keep doing the morning milking myself as long as the old parlour stood. If they bought the robot anyway, I'd let Kofi run it and I'd stay on the fields and the youngstock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, more like hearing a noise in the barn at night and not wanting to go check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a younger manager in the wings would sting. Who's that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody yet. But the board chair's nephew has just finished a farm management course, and he talks about data like it's feed. I'm not jealous, I'm just tired. I don't want my last five years to be about proving I'm not a dinosaur.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Bev in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit that keeps me up. Bev would retire, I think, if the parlour went robotic. She's got a bad shoulder and she'd say it's a sign. But she'd be retiring because of a machine, not because she chose to, and I'd feel I let her down.

S1.say: I'd tell the co-op we need a plan for the crew before a plan for the machines. At the union I'd push for new kit on co-op farms to come with training and no job losses for the first few years.
S1.think: I think the robot milker comes in and I'm the one stuck managing something I don't trust. A younger, keener manager would be waiting, and that would sting more than I'd say out loud.
S1.do: Asks the board for a written promise protecting the crew before any purchase, and brings the union rep to the vote. Keeps doing morning milking herself as long as the old parlour stands, and hands any robot to her younger colleague while she stays on fields and youngstock.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a noise in the barn at night she doesn't want to go and check.
S1.quote: I don't want my last five years to be about proving I'm not a dinosaur.
S1.fieldNote: Her first move is collective: the union, a written promise, the vote. Personally she isn't at risk of hardship, so the worry is pride and loyalty to Bev rather than money. There's a gap between her public line about the crew and her private fear of being sidelined.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's not a change, that's a flood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need laws before machines, and we haven't got them. At the union I'd be loud. I'd say no farm that takes public money should be allowed to sack its crew for robots without paying them properly and retraining them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally? I'd be all right, and I know it. House is paid, pension's decent, Luis has his job. But Fernhill without people isn't a farm I want to run. I'd go before I'd switch them on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd sit down with Luis and do the sums for stopping at sixty instead of sixty-three. I'd go to every union meeting and write to our member of parliament, which I've never done, about the crew. When the robots arrived on the farm I'd hand in my notice, but only after making sure Kofi and Bev had the best deal I could fight for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not for myself. More like watching a storm come up the valley when you know half the sheep are still out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be all right. Two years is very short warning. What does having only two years change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means there's no time to train anyone. With two years I can't help Kofi learn a new trade, and Bev hasn't got time to reach her full pension. If I had longer I'd use it for them, not me. Two years just means I watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the crew the day you hand in your notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm sorry it's me leaving and not the machine. Then I'd probably make a joke about the robot needing to learn to swear at the gate latch. I'd do the last milking myself, by hand where I can, just so it's done properly once more.

S2.say: I'd say we need laws before machines and we don't have them. Any farm on public money shouldn't be allowed to sack its crew for robots without proper pay and retraining.
S2.think: I'd be fine personally, with the house paid off, a decent pension and Luis working. But a farm without people isn't one I want to run, and I'd leave before I'd switch the robots on.
S2.do: Does the sums with her partner to stop work at sixty instead of sixty-three. Goes to every union meeting and writes to her member of parliament for the first time, and hands in her notice when robots arrive after fighting for the best deal for her crew.
S2.feel: Anxious for her crew rather than herself, like a storm coming up the valley with sheep still out.
S2.quote: I'd say I'm sorry it's me leaving and not the machine.
S2.fieldNote: With two years she sees no way to help anyone retrain, and that helplessness drives her mood more than her own safety. She becomes politically active for the first time. Her resistance shows as refusal: she'd retire rather than run an automated farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd be sixty-three. That's when I'd planned to stop anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's use them properly. At the branch I'd want the union to set up a fund or a course so the younger farmhands can move into something before the robots arrive. I'd say that loudly, because five years is enough to do something if people start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it means I get out just about on time. I'd hand over the keys around when the machines come in, so I'd never have to manage one. That's lucky, and I know it's luck, not cleverness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job exactly as now, no robot on my watch. I'd push the co-op to pay for Kofi to do a course, maybe machinery maintenance, so he's the one fixing the robots and not replaced by them. And I'd help Bev work out how to bridge the two years to her pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but with a plan, which is better than the fast one. It feels like knowing a dry spring is coming and having time to buy in feed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years change compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything for the crew, not much for me. With five years Kofi can retrain and Bev can reach sixty-five-ish. With two, I'm just writing angry letters. I'd still be resisting the machine, but I'd have time to do something useful with the anger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd never use these machines yourself. If the co-op asked you to stay on to train the next manager, would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay to teach them the cows, not the computer. Somebody has to tell them that Number 47 kicks on the left and hates the yellow gate. If the robot needs that, it'll have to learn it from me over a cup of tea, the old way.

S3.say: I'd tell the union branch we've got a few years and should use them, with a fund or course so younger farmhands can move into something before the robots arrive.
S3.think: I'd get out about on time and never have to manage one of these machines. That's luck, not cleverness, and I know it.
S3.do: Keeps working as now with no robot on her watch while pushing the co-op to pay for her colleague Kofi to train in machinery maintenance. Helps Bev plan how to bridge the gap to her pension.
S3.feel: Uneasy but steadier than the fast picture, like seeing a dry spring coming with time to buy feed.
S3.quote: Somebody has to tell them that Number 47 kicks on the left and hates the yellow gate.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lines up with her planned retirement, so the extra time turns her anger into useful action for the crew. She still refuses to touch the technology but would pass on animal knowledge. Her sense of luck is honest and a little guilty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be sixty-eight and long gone from the parlour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty of time for the government to get it right, so no excuses. At the union I'd want a proper plan for rural jobs, not some leaflet. I'd say young people should be told now which trades will still need hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it hardly touches me. I'd retire at sixty-three as planned and probably grow vegetables on Mill Lane. What bothers me is that I'd be watching from the side while Kofi and his lot work it out, and I'd have no say any more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal until sixty-three and hand Fernhill over to whoever comes next, with my notebooks. I'd stay in the union as a retired member and go to meetings. When it arrived I'd be at the fence with the other old ones, having opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy in a faraway way. Like reading about a flood in a different valley, where you know people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your children anything in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Pablo to keep fixing bikes, because people will always want someone real to talk to about their bike. And Inés is a nurse, so I'd tell her to get into the union properly. I'd be the mother who sends newspaper cuttings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd never touch the machines. With ten years, might you try one before you retire?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd be sixty-three and stubborn by then, worse than now. Kofi can show me on his phone and I'll nod. Some things you're allowed to skip at my age.

S4.say: I'd say a decade is plenty of time for government to get it right, so there are no excuses. I'd want a proper plan for rural jobs and young people told now which trades will still need hands.
S4.think: It hardly touches me, as I'd retire at sixty-three and grow vegetables. What bothers me is watching from the side while the younger crew works it out without me.
S4.do: Carries on as normal until sixty-three, then hands Fernhill over with her notebooks. Stays in the union as a retired member and keeps going to meetings.
S4.feel: Uneasy in a distant way, like hearing about a flood in a valley where she knows people.
S4.quote: I'd tell Pablo to keep fixing bikes, because people will always want someone real to talk to about their bike.
S4.fieldNote: The ten-year picture lands after her retirement, so it barely touches her income. She still won't try the technology even with time, which is consistent with her resistance. Her worry shifts to having no voice and to her children.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, because there's no time for the crew. What would help is a law that says if a farm brings in robots, it pays the workers it lets go a proper sum and pays for their training. Not a handout, a debt the farm owes them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the cows. Everyone talks about jobs, but a cow knows when the person who milks her is gone. I'm not saying that stops anything. I just want someone to write it down.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about jobs, but a cow knows when the person who milks her is gone.
portrait: Hana Reyes is 58 and has managed Fernhill, a cooperative dairy and grain farm, for fourteen years, leading a crew of six. She knows every cow by her walk, keeps records on paper and has never used AI tools. Financially she is secure, with a paid-off house and a decent pension, so her worries are about her crew, her pride and the animals rather than money. In the mild pictures she simply carries on, and as change speeds up she turns to the union and politics and would retire rather than run robots herself. The ten-year picture lands after her planned retirement, which leaves her uneasy but mostly a spectator.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there would be no time for her crew to retrain or reach their pensions.
whatWouldHelp: A law making farms that bring in robots pay the workers they let go a proper sum and fund their training, which she sees as a debt owed rather than a handout.
